metadata.note: The Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railroad (Petaluma & Santa Rosa Railway until the 1918 foreclosure reorganisation): a 600 V DC electric interurban in Sonoma County, CA, built 1904-05 from the San Francisco steamer landing at Petaluma north to Sebastopol, with lines from Sebastopol east to Santa Rosa and north through Graton to Forestville, plus a 1913 branch from Liberty to Two Rock. Company-owned stern-wheel steamers (Gold, Petaluma) carried passengers and freight between Petaluma and San Francisco. Drawn as five features because each ran its own service (Borden gives separate daily round-trip counts for Petaluma-Sebastopol, Sebastopol-Santa Rosa and Sebastopol-Forestville) and because the Fourth Street run in downtown Santa Rosa ended six months before the rest. All rail passenger service ended Jun 30 1932; the railroad survived as a freight carrier (electric to 1946-47, then diesel) under Northwestern Pacific / Southern Pacific ownership into the 1980s, which is deliberately not drawn (Rule 1). The horsecar lines the company bought in 1903 in Petaluma and Santa Rosa are not drawn (Rule 5); only Fourth Street in Santa Rosa was ever electrified, from 1905.
metadata.replaces: This file replaces feature psr-petaluma-santa-rosa, formerly in northwestern_pacific_santa_rosa.geojson: a 3-point straight-line sketch Petaluma-Sebastopol-Santa Rosa coloured in the Northwestern Pacific's #386641. That colour was a Rule 4 error - the P&SR ran its own trains under its own name until passenger service ended, and the NWP only took formal ownership of the stock on Feb 26 1932, four months before the end.
metadata.ownership_note: Rule 4 judgment: one company, one colour (#B5838D) for 1904-1932, no split. Southern Pacific and Santa Fe money bought the P&SR common stock through the Anglo-California Trust Co. on Jun 27 1928 (SP took Santa Fe's half on Jan 17 1929), and the Northwestern Pacific - itself SP-controlled - acquired the stock outright on Feb 26 1932 after ICC approval on Jan 22 1932; P&SR president Maggard had been made president of the NWP. Throughout, the Petaluma & Santa Rosa remained a separate operating company running its own cars under its own name, so this is stock control, not a change of who ran the trains. No passenger train ran under NWP operation, so there is no NWP-coloured era to draw.
sources: Stanley T. Borden, 'Petaluma & Santa Rosa Electric R.R.', The Western Railroader vol. 23 no. 4, issue 244 (April 1960) - corporate history, construction dates, daily round-trip counts for 1915 and 1927, speeds, 1946-47 track changes, station list: https://archive.org/details/sim_western-railroader-the-western-railfan_1960-04_23_4

Robert Ellison and Walt Sievers, 'Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railroad Company', The Western Railroader vol. 15 no. 4, issue 148 (February 1952): https://archive.org/details/sim_western-railroader-the-western-railfan_1952-02_15_4
Wikipedia, Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railroad (milepost table, dates): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petaluma_and_Santa_Rosa_Railroad
Wikipedia, Joe Rodota Trail (trail on the P&SR roadbed): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Rodota_Trail
source_conflicts: Opening of regular service: Nov 29 1904 (Borden 1960, 'first regular train schedule going into effect') vs Dec 1 1904 (Ellison & Sievers 1952; Wikipedia). Both are 1904; segment years unaffected.

End of rail passenger service: 'on June 30, 1932, all passenger service was discontinued' (Borden) vs 'On July 1st ... all passenger service on the rail line was abandoned' (Ellison & Sievers; Wikipedia). Read as last day Jun 30, first day without trains Jul 1. abandonedrails.com says trolley service ceased 1933 - that is the year the cars were retired (Apr 22 1933), not the end of service. A Petaluma Argus-Courier / Petaluma360 summary says passenger service ended in 1935 - that is the steamers, not the trains.
Two Rock branch passenger end: Sep 20 1925 (Borden) vs Sep 30 1925 (Ellison & Sievers; Wikipedia).
NWP purchase: 1928 (abandonedrails.com; the SP/Santa Fe trust purchase of the stock) vs 1932 (Borden; Ellison & Sievers; Wikipedia: NWP acquisition of the stock). Recorded in ownership_note.

Fourth Street dismantling: Wikipedia says McDonald Ave-Olive St was dismantled in 1931; Borden says operation ended Dec 31 1931 and rail removal was completed May 31 1932. The drawn end year 1931 is the last year of service either way.
not_yet_sourced: Every headway_min is derived from Borden's 1915 and 1927 daily round-trip counts or guessed (1904, Two Rock); no timetable was read. The Jan 1 1932 public timetable reproduced in both Western Railroader articles is an image whose archive.org OCR is unreadable; reading it would give real frequencies and running times.
avg_speed_kmh is an estimate from Borden's 30-35 mph maximum; no running time found.

Exact track position in Petaluma between the steamer wharf/depot (Washington and Copeland streets) and the surviving spur north of Lakeville Street, and whether trains used the 1922 'West Petaluma extension' or the Petaluma Creek west-bank spur (both appear to be freight spurs; not drawn).
Exact street routing through Sebastopol (Gravenstein Hwy S / Petaluma Ave / Main St are inferred).
Location of Leddy junction - drawn at North Wright Road on mileage evidence; the US Navy airfield that Borden places 'at Leddy' could pin it down.
Whether all Sebastopol-Santa Rosa cars ran through to the McDonald Avenue terminus on Fourth Street.
Two Rock branch frequency, and its alignment for the first 1.2 mi west of Liberty.
metadata.geometry_quality: All five features are traced from real geometry except one labelled 1.2 mi straight leg at the east end of the Two Rock branch. Main line 16.80 mi vs 16.66 documented; Sebastopol-Santa Rosa 6.77 vs 6.7; Sebastopol-Forestville 7.42 vs 7.1; Fourth Street 1.05 vs 'slightly over a mile'; Two Rock 5.33 vs 5.3-5.77. About 5.9 mi in all is drawn on road geometry standing in for street and side-of-road running (Copeland St, Gravenstein Hwy S / Petaluma Ave into Sebastopol, Main St through Sebastopol, Sebastopol Rd / Sebastopol Ave / Olive St into Santa Rosa); each feature's geometry_quality names its legs. Sources: OpenStreetMap ways named 'Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railroad' (TIGER-derived), the Joe Rodota and West County rail-trails, OSM roads, and one OpenHistoricalMap way (Fourth Street). Despike, reversal and revisit checks run clean on every feature.

properties.line: Petaluma and Santa Rosa: Petaluma – Sebastopol
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. Borden (1960) gives the 1927 maximum passenger speed as 30-35 mph; no published end-to-end running time was found (the Jan 1 1932 public timetable reproduced in both Western Railroader articles is an image whose OCR is unreadable). An average of about 20 mph (32 km/h) allowing for stops and street running in Petaluma and Sebastopol is assumed.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 16.8 mi against a documented 16.66 mi (Borden's milepost for Sebastopol; Wikipedia gives 16.7). 14.5 mi follows OpenStreetMap ways named 'Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railroad' - the TIGER-derived abandoned grade from north Petaluma to Alten (MP 14.9), plus 0.8 mi of surviving P&SR-operated spur and siding track (Park Siding) along the west bank of the Petaluma River. APPROXIMATED ON ROADS (about 2.2 mi): 0.4 mi on Copeland Street from the steamer wharf at its foot to Lakeville Street, standing in for the line between the wharf/depot (Washington and Copeland) and the surviving spur - the exact track position is not documented; and 1.9 mi from Alten into the Sebastopol depot (261 S. Main St.) along Gravenstein Highway South and Petaluma Avenue, where the mapped grade runs into the highway - the P&SR was street and side-of-road running in Sebastopol, but that it used exactly these streets is inferred, not sourced. Connectors between OSM fragments total 0.07 mi. No straight-line legs.

segments.note: Petaluma & Santa Rosa Railway: first spike Apr 5 1904 at the steamer Gold landing at the foot of Copeland Street; the first passenger car reached Sebastopol in October 1904 and the first regular schedule took effect Nov 29 1904 (Borden; Ellison & Sievers and Wikipedia say Dec 1). Trains met the company's own San Francisco steamers at Petaluma. Reorganised as the Petaluma & Santa Rosa Railroad after foreclosure on Oct 29 1918 - same line, same operator. Ridership peaked at 760,725 in 1912. In 1915 the cars made 12 daily round trips Petaluma-Sebastopol (Borden). HEADWAY IS AN ESTIMATE: 85 min is that 1915 count spread over a ~17-hour day and applied back to 1904; earlier frequencies are not sourced.
sources: Segment-level: dates in this note are from Borden, 'Petaluma & Santa Rosa Electric R.R.', The Western Railroader 23:4 (April 1960), and Ellison & Sievers, The Western Railroader 15:4 (Feb 1952); the headway is an ESTIMATE derived from Borden's daily round-trip counts, not read from a timetable.

segments.note: A county highway paralleling much of the line was completed in 1921 and passenger revenue fell from then on (Borden). In 1927 the cars made 11 daily round trips Petaluma-Sebastopol, all single-car trains. Rail passengers fell from 491,672 in 1922 to 162,742 in 1931. Southern Pacific and Santa Fe money bought control through the Anglo-California Trust Co. on Jun 27 1928, and the Northwestern Pacific took formal ownership of the stock on Feb 26 1932 after ICC approval on Jan 22, but the P&SR kept running its own trains under its own name; all rail passenger service ended Jun 30 1932 (Borden; Ellison & Sievers and Wikipedia give Jul 1, the first day without service). Freight - electric to 1946-47, then diesel - continued for decades and is deliberately not drawn (Rule 1); steamer passengers lasted to 1935. HEADWAY IS AN ESTIMATE: 95 min is the 1927 count of 11 round trips over a ~17-hour day.

properties.line: Petaluma and Santa Rosa: Sebastopol – Santa Rosa
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. Borden (1960) gives the 1927 maximum passenger speed as 30-35 mph; no published end-to-end running time was found (the Jan 1 1932 public timetable reproduced in both Western Railroader articles is an image whose OCR is unreadable). An average of about 20 mph (32 km/h) allowing for stops and street running in Petaluma and Sebastopol is assumed.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 6.77 mi against a documented 6.7 mi (Wikipedia: Sebastopol MP 16.7 to Santa Rosa MP 23.4; Borden's table gives Sebastopol 16.66). 3.6 mi follows the Joe Rodota Trail (with 0.2 mi of OSM way still named 'Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railroad') from the Sebastopol depot east to North Wright Road - this stretch is the P&SR's own grade, which it kept until the 1980s. At Wright Road the line is drawn turning south onto Sebastopol Road along the short trail spur there; that spur as the Leddy junction is INFERRED from the mileage (Leddy MP 20.2 is 3.5 mi from Sebastopol, and the trail reaches Wright Road at 3.5 mi). From Leddy to the Northwestern Pacific crossing the P&SR was 'street and side of the road running' along Sebastopol Avenue (Borden), so 2.6 mi is drawn on today's Sebastopol Road, then 0.6 mi on Sebastopol Avenue, Olive Street, Railroad Street and Wilson Street to the depot at Fourth and Wilson (Borden: 'Sebastopol Ave. to Olive St., Olive to Fourth St.'). LATER-ALIGNMENT TRAP AVOIDED: east of Wright Road the Joe Rodota Trail follows the Northwestern Pacific's Sebastopol branch, which the P&SR's freight trains only used from Oct 20 1947, after its own Sebastopol Avenue track was lifted in 1946-47; that is not drawn here. No straight-line legs.

segments.note: Regular service began Nov 29 / Dec 1 1904 from Petaluma via Sebastopol to the California Northwestern crossing on Sebastopol Avenue at the Santa Rosa city limits, where the steam road refused to let the electric line cross. From Jan 4 1905 a car hauled over the steam tracks by horses waited on the far side and passengers walked across the gap; on Mar 1 1905 the 'Battle of Sebastopol Avenue' was fought over the crossing, and shortly after midnight the first car ran into downtown Santa Rosa under its own power (Borden; Ellison & Sievers). The drawn line reaches the 4th & Wilson depot, a few hundred yards beyond the 1904 railhead. HEADWAY IS AN ESTIMATE: no 1904 frequency is published; 60 min is assumed.

segments.note: Through service into downtown Santa Rosa from March 1905, the cars continuing along Fourth Street to McDonald Avenue (see the separate Fourth Street feature). In 1915 the cars made 19 daily round trips Sebastopol-Santa Rosa (Borden), the busiest part of the system; from 1919 an express trailer was handled on some trips. HEADWAY IS AN ESTIMATE: 55 min is the 1915 count over a ~17-hour day.

segments.note: Paralleling county highway completed 1921. In 1927 the cars made 18 daily round trips Sebastopol-Santa Rosa, two of them handling an express trailer; a new Santa Rosa passenger and freight depot was built in 1927. Interurban cars stopped running east of the depot on Dec 31 1931, and all rail passenger service ended Jun 30 1932 (Borden; Ellison & Sievers and Wikipedia say Jul 1) under the new Northwestern Pacific ownership (stock acquired Feb 26 1932; the P&SR still ran its own trains). The Sebastopol Avenue track survived for freight until 1946-47 - not drawn (Rule 1). HEADWAY IS AN ESTIMATE: 57 min is the 1927 count over a ~17-hour day.

properties.line: Petaluma and Santa Rosa: Fourth Street (Santa Rosa)
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. Street running through downtown Santa Rosa past Courthouse Square; no running time was found. 15 km/h is assumed for a one-mile city-street run.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 1.05 mi against a documented 'slightly over a mile on Fourth to the terminus at McDonald Ave.' (Borden). Geometry is OpenHistoricalMap way 198305780 ('Fourth Street', CC0, geometry only - its 1854 start date is a placeholder and is not used), an 8-vertex line drawn straight down Fourth Street, which is itself straight. Today's Fourth Street is cut by US 101 and the Santa Rosa Plaza mall, so the drawn line crosses both; that is the historical street, not an error. No straight-line legs beyond the street's own straightness.

segments.note: The P&SR laid its line 'for slightly over a mile on Fourth to the terminus at McDonald Ave.' in 1905 (Borden), on the street where the Santa Rosa Street Railway had run horsecars since 1878 - the P&SR bought the horsecar companies for their franchises and electrified only Fourth Street; the horsecar era is not drawn (Rule 5). Interurban cars from Sebastopol ran through to the terminus. Operation between the depot at Olive Street and McDonald Avenue ended Dec 31 1931 and the rails were gone by May 31 1932 (Borden; Wikipedia: dismantled 1931). HEADWAY IS AN ESTIMATE: 55 min assumes the Sebastopol-Santa Rosa cars (19 round trips in 1915, 18 in 1927) all ran through to McDonald Avenue, which is not confirmed.

properties.line: Petaluma and Santa Rosa: Sebastopol – Forestville
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. Borden (1960) gives the 1927 maximum passenger speed as 30-35 mph; no published end-to-end running time was found (the Jan 1 1932 public timetable reproduced in both Western Railroader articles is an image whose OCR is unreadable). properties.geometry_quality: Traced 7.42 mi against a documented 7.1 mi (Sebastopol MP 16.7 to Forestville MP 23.8; Ellison & Sievers say 7 miles). 6.9 mi follows the West County Trail and OSM ways still named 'Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railroad' along the abandoned grade from the north edge of Sebastopol through Graton to Forestville. APPROXIMATED ON STREETS: 0.5 mi from the Sebastopol depot north along South and North Main Street to where the trail begins at Analysis Avenue - the P&SR ran in the streets of Sebastopol, but this exact routing is inferred. Connectors 0.04 mi. No straight-line legs.

segments.note: Built north from Sebastopol: service reached Green Valley (later Graton) on Jan 26 1905 and the first car reached Forestville on Jul 15 1905 (Borden; Ellison & Sievers). The 1905 Graton-only months are inside this segment; the drawn line runs to Forestville from the start. In 1915 the cars made 16 daily round trips Sebastopol-Forestville (Borden). HEADWAY IS AN ESTIMATE: 65 min is the 1915 count over a ~17-hour day.

segments.note: In 1927 the cars made 15 daily round trips Sebastopol-Forestville; two cars were converted to one-man operation for this run in 1929 (Borden). All rail passenger service ended Jun 30 1932 (Borden; others give Jul 1). The line carried fruit freight for decades afterwards, cut back to Ross in 1961 and to the Sebastopol Apple Growers' Union plant in 1969 - not drawn (Rule 1). HEADWAY IS AN ESTIMATE: 70 min is the 1927 count over a ~17-hour day.

properties.line: Petaluma and Santa Rosa: Two Rock Branch
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. Borden (1960) gives the 1927 maximum passenger speed as 30-35 mph; no published end-to-end running time was found (the Jan 1 1932 public timetable reproduced in both Western Railroader articles is an image whose OCR is unreadable). properties.geometry_quality: Traced 5.33 mi against a documented 5.77 mi (Borden) / 5.3 mi (Wikipedia: Liberty MP 5.1 to Two Rock MP 10.4). 4.1 mi follows the OSM way named 'Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railroad' (TIGER-derived abandoned grade) from east of Cherry to Two Rock. STRAIGHT-LINE LEG: the first 1.2 mi, from the main line at Liberty (MP 5.1, located on the traced main line) due west to the start of the mapped grade, is a ruled line - OSM has nothing there.

segments.note: The 5.77-mile branch from Liberty to Two Rock opened Jul 28 1913, at a cost of $91,741.96 (Borden; Ellison & Sievers). The 1921 county highway hit it hardest; passenger revenue fell from $400 to $27 a month and passenger service ended in September 1925 - Sep 20 per Borden, Sep 30 per Ellison & Sievers and Wikipedia. Freight continued to 1952 and is not drawn (Rule 1). HEADWAY IS AN ESTIMATE: no branch frequency is published anywhere found; 180 min is a guess for a lightly used rural branch.
